stories.headline: S&P 500, NASDAQ-100 SLIP OFF RECORD HIGHS AS 10-YEAR YIELD TICKS BACK UP TO 5.28%
stories.body: The S&P 500 eased 0.22% to 7,802 and the Nasdaq-100 fell 0.21% to 31,160, giving back a slice of Monday's record close near 7,819 after the 10-year Treasury yield edged 1 bp higher to 5.28%, still within shouting distance of its highest level since 2007.
stories.explain: A 1-basis-point move looks trivial, but it's happening after the yield already failed to hold a modest pullback from 5.27% — a sign that the term premium investors demand for long-duration risk isn't coming down even as the acute oil-shock story fades. Richly valued mega-cap tech carries the most duration risk in the index because so much of its value sits in cash flows far in the future, so even small upward wobbles in the discount rate show up disproportionately in the Nasdaq-100.

stories.headline: FED HOLDS AT 3.75%-4% RANGE AS MARKETS AWAIT THIS WEEK'S CPI AND INFLATION-EXPECTATIONS READ
stories.body: The fed funds rate remains at 3.75%-4% following September's hike into the Strait of Hormuz oil shock, with traders now treating this week's CPI print and the University of Michigan inflation-expectations survey as the next real test of whether that hike was sufficient.
stories.explain: The Fed's September move was aimed at expectations, not the current price level — inflation caused by a supply disruption can't be fixed by raising rates, but a central bank can use rate hikes to signal it won't let a one-time shock become a permanent one. September's Michigan survey put year-ahead expectations at 4.6%; a reading that climbs further this week would argue the hike wasn't enough and the 10-year's term premium has further to rise, while a stabilizing print would validate the Fed's bet and open room for the yield relief markets have been pricing in fits and starts.

stories.headline: OIL EASES TO $89 AS HORMUZ RISK PREMIUM CONTINUES TO FADE; GOLD RETREATS TO $4,132
stories.body: WTI crude fell 1.41% to roughly $89, extending its pullback from last week's post-closure spike above $93, while gold dropped 0.91% to $4,132 as a firming dollar made the metal more expensive for foreign buyers.
stories.explain: Oil and gold are moving for related but distinct reasons: crude is sliding because tanker traffic through the strait is normalizing, directly easing the supply-shock premium, while gold is giving ground because the dollar's bounce raises gold's price in every other currency and makes competing dollar assets marginally more attractive. Both moves are consistent with markets pricing the acute phase of the shock as past, even though the inflation it already generated is still working through the CPI data the Fed is waiting on.

stories.headline: DOLLAR INDEX CLIMBS TO 102.25 AS HAVEN FLOWS RETURN AFTER LAST WEEK'S PULLBACK
stories.body: The DXY rose 0.22% to 102.25, recovering ground after slipping to 101.85 last week, as some of the safety bid tied to European fiscal jitters crept back into the dollar even without a fresh catalyst.
stories.explain: The dollar's moves this month have had less to do with the U.S. economic picture and more to do with relative safety — capital flows toward the deepest, most liquid market during any bout of European sovereign stress, and dollars and Treasuries are still that market even with U.S. yields near two-decade highs. A bounce back toward 102 without new U.S. data suggests today's move is a continuation of that relative-safety trade rather than a fresh vote of confidence in the Fed's path.

stories.headline: ST. JOHN'S LOSES GUARD DONNIE FREEMAN FOR THE SEASON TO ACHILLES INJURY BEFORE TIP-OFF
stories.body: Rising junior guard Donnie Freeman underwent surgery for a non-contact Achilles injury suffered in a team workout, ruling him out for all of 2026-27 before the season even begins. Coach Rick Pitino called it a major blow to the Red Storm's depth heading into Big East play, which opens in November, while Duke enters the year as a popular preseason pick after adding a deep transfer and freshman class under coach Jon Scheyer.

stories.headline: LAKERS' REPORTED $12 BILLION SALE HEADLINES PRESEASON AS LEBRON DEBUTS WITH SIXERS
stories.body: A reported $12 billion sale of the Lakers — a North American sports-franchise record — is the backdrop to a 67-game preseason slate now underway league-wide. LeBron James opened his 24th season with his fourth franchise after signing with Philadelphia, pairing with Jaylen Brown, Joel Embiid, and Tyrese Maxey.

stories.headline: FALCONS' JAMES PEARCE JR. SUSPENDED 8 GAMES FOR CONDUCT POLICY VIOLATION
stories.body: Atlanta edge rusher James Pearce Jr. was suspended eight games without pay for violating the NFL's personal-conduct policy, a significant loss for the Falcons' pass rush. The league is also reviewing possible discipline for 49ers owner Jed York following his arrest in Ohio, adding a second integrity headache in the same week.

stories.headline: OHIO STATE'S JEREMIAH SMITH SETS PROGRAM RECORDS AS THE SENATE PASSES THE PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT
stories.body: Ohio State receiver Jeremiah Smith broke the program's career receptions and touchdown records last weekend, while Alabama's 56-23 rout of Mississippi State and Missouri's 45-17 upset of Florida were the week's signature results. Off the field, the Senate passed the Protect College Sports Act 77-22 Friday, setting a uniform national NIL standard and protecting Olympic-sport scholarships, with backers pushing for a House vote before Election Day. The slate is quiet until Friday, when No. 20 Iowa visits No. 18 Washington.

sports.detail: Fell to 3-1 (0-1 Big Ten) in a road loss at No. 18 USC Saturday. Punter Hunter Green was named to the Ray Guy Award's "Ray's 8" for Week Five. Next: host No. 20 Iowa at Husky Stadium Friday, Oct. 9 — the Hawkeyes' first trip to Montlake in 63 years.

Added former Oregon assistant Mike Mennenga to the staff and brought in transfers Harun Zrno, Steele Venters, and others to pair with returning leading scorer Wesley Yates III. First look comes in an exhibition at Boise State Oct. 17, before hosting rival Washington State Oct. 25.

Beat the Chargers 30-23 Sunday to improve to 3-1, bouncing back from a loss to Washington the week before. Sam Darnold threw for 168 yards and two touchdowns and jumped 51 spots to No. 21 in the NFL's new Top 100 rankings. Next: host San Francisco Sunday, Oct. 11.

Beat Phoenix 109-91 in Monday's preseason opener at Little Caesars Arena; Cade Cunningham led with 25 points and 12 rebounds. Center Jalen Duren ended his restricted free-agency standoff this week, signing a fully guaranteed five-year, $200 million deal just ahead of the qualifying-offer deadline and rejoining the roster for camp. Next: at Washington Wizards Oct. 10.

Closed the season 73-85, missing the playoffs for the first time since 2019 — a stunning reversal after last year's Game 7 ALCS run. GM Jerry Dipoto confirmed the club "will go outside to hire our manager" after Torey Lovullo, a leading candidate, re-signed with Arizona instead.

deepDive.title: The Term Premium: Why a 5.28% 10-Year Isn't Just About Fed Expectations
content: Today's brief has the 10-year Treasury yield ticking up another basis point to 5.28%, even as the acute driver of this cycle — the Strait of Hormuz oil shock — keeps fading, with WTI down to $89 from above $93. If the long-term yield just reflected where investors expect the fed funds rate to average over the next decade, it should be easing in step with oil and the Fed's own signals that September's hike may be enough. It isn't, and the gap between what simple rate expectations predict and what the market is actually charging is called the term premium — and right now it's doing most of the work keeping the 10-year this high.

The 10-year yield can be decomposed into two pieces: the average expected path of short-term rates over the life of the bond, and a term premium that compensates investors for the risk of holding a 10-year bond instead of just rolling over short-term Treasuries. The New York Fed's ACM model is the standard way economists estimate this split, and it typically finds the term premium adds anywhere from zero to over 100 basis points depending on the environment. When the term premium rises, it means investors are demanding extra compensation for duration risk itself — uncertainty about future inflation, future Treasury issuance, and how reliably the bond will hold its value — separate from whatever they think the Fed will actually do with the funds rate.

What gets missed is that a rising term premium is often a signal about fiscal and institutional credibility, not just inflation math. The clearest precedent is 1994, when the 10-year yield jumped more than 200 basis points over the year even as the Fed's hikes were well-telegraphed, because investors repriced the premium for holding long-duration paper amid heavy Treasury issuance and inflation uncertainty — a move nicknamed the "bond market massacre." Heavy issuance to fund deficits, like the kind the U.S. is running now, tends to push the term premium up mechanically: more supply of long bonds requires a higher yield to clear the market, independent of where the Fed sets overnight rates.

That framing changes how to read this week's setup. If the CPI print and Michigan survey come in soft, expectations for the funds rate can fall while the term premium stays elevated — meaning the 10-year, and the mortgage and corporate borrowing costs tied to it, may not fall nearly as much as a rate-expectations-only view would suggest. For a portfolio, that argues for treating the 10-year's stickiness above 5% as partly structural — tied to issuance and duration-risk appetite — rather than purely a referendum on whether the Fed's September hike was the right call.
